# The desk

Four AI agents judge every setup the rules find (about 2 to 3 a day across the Nasdaq, S&P 500, Dow and Russell 2000): [[Scout]], [[Sceptic]], [[Risk]] and [[Chief]]. Each thinks separately, with its own memory. The Chief decides take or skip.

The desk only works live, never on old prices, because an AI has already read about the past. Every setup is played out whether the desk takes it or not, so its picks can be scored against simply taking everything.

This is the experiment behind the question: **can an AI trade?**

See also [[Home]] and [[Questions]].

An obvious high or low where traders put their stop orders. The theory is that the market takes out these stops before making the real move. The site logs each bait level and whether it got taken.

# Buying low, selling high

Split yesterday's range in half. Selling makes more sense in the top half and buying in the bottom half. Traders call this premium and discount. It adds to a setup's [[Grades|grade]] but isn't a strict rule.

# Grades

Every setup gets a score out of 100 *before* we know how it turns out: level quality 25, [[SMT]] 15, how big the trend-flip candle was 20, hourly trend agreeing 15, [[Buying low, selling high]] 10, time of day 10, gap and order block overlapping 5. A++ is 85 or more, A+ 72, A 60, B 45, otherwise C. If higher grades don't actually win more, the [[Edge report]] will say so.

# Highs and lows

The turning points on a chart. Higher highs and higher lows mean an uptrend; lower highs and lower lows mean a downtrend. A turning point only counts once two more candles have closed after it, so the site never uses [[No peeking at the future|information from the future]].

title: Key levels
text:

type: idea

# Key levels

Highs and lows on the chart where lots of traders have probably left stop orders. The big ones are [[Session levels]]: yesterday's high and low, last week's, and the Asia and London ranges. When two highs (or lows) are almost equal, even more stops pile up there.

The [[The main strategy|main strategy]] only cares about the important ones. When price pokes past one and comes back, that's a [[Sweep]].

# SMT

The Nasdaq and the S&P 500 normally move together, and so do gold and silver. If the Nasdaq makes a new high but the S&P 500 doesn't, they disagree. Traders call this SMT, and it's a hint the move is fake and about to reverse.

It's one of the checks in [[The main strategy]]. The [[Edge report]] tests whether it actually helps.

# Session levels

The most important [[Key levels]]: **PDH and PDL** (yesterday's high and low), **PWH and PWL** (last week's), and the high and low of the **Asia** session (8pm to midnight) and **London** session (2am to 5am), all New York time.

## My notes

title: Skipped trades
text:
---
type: idea
---
# Skipped trades

When a possible trade fails one of the checks, it's skipped, and the reason is written down. If there was still a trade to be had, the site plays it out in the background anyway. That way we can see whether each rule is saving money or costing it. Results are in the [[Edge report]].

%% my notes below. Argon never changes anything under this line %%
## My notes

title: Sweep
text:
---
type: idea
---
# Sweep

Price pokes just past a [[Key levels|key level]] and comes straight back. The idea is that big players pushed price there on purpose to trigger everyone's stop orders, then reversed.

If price pushes through and *stays* there instead, it's a breakout, not a sweep, and the strategy doesn't trade it. Only sweeps during [[Trading hours]] count. The candle that did the poking is a [[Big push candle]].

%% my notes below. Argon never changes anything under this line %%
## My notes

title: The main strategy
text:
---
type: idea
---
# The main strategy

The main strategy has a list of checks, in order. Every one must pass:

1. An important [[Key levels|level]] to target
2. A [[Sweep]] during [[Trading hours]], not a breakout
3. Matches the day's direction, when that check is switched on
4. The other market disagrees ([[SMT]]), when that check is switched on
5. A [[Trend flip]] within 40 minutes
6. Price comes back to the [[Price gap (FVG)|gap]] or [[Order block]] within an hour
7. It passes the risk rules from Argon v1

The stop goes just past the sweep. The target is the next level on the other side, if it's worth at least twice the risk. Anything that fails a check is a [[Skipped trades|skipped trade]]. The full rules are in [[Rulebook v1.0]].

## My notes

title: The order-block strategy
text:
---
type: idea
---
# The order-block strategy

A second, simpler strategy, kept separate from [[The main strategy]]. It buys or sells the first time price comes back to a fresh 15-minute [[Order block]] during [[Trading hours]], as long as the hourly trend agrees. Stop just past the block, target twice the risk or the next level.

## My notes

title: Trading hours
text:
---
type: idea
---
# Trading hours

The strategies only trade in two windows: London 2am to 5am and New York 8:30 to 11:30am (New York time). The New York open is where the biggest traps tend to happen.

## My notes

title: Trend break
text:
---
type: idea
---
# Trend break

Price closes past the last turning point. If that's in the same direction as the trend, the trend has continued. If it's the opposite way, the trend may be turning. A turn made with a [[Big push candle]] is a [[Trend flip]].

%% my notes below. Argon never changes anything under this line %%
## My notes

title: Trend flip
text:
---
type: idea
---
# Trend flip

The trend changes direction with one big, decisive candle. This is one of the checks in [[The main strategy]]: after a [[Sweep]], the trend has to flip within 40 minutes. A fast move like this usually leaves a [[Price gap (FVG)]] or an [[Order block]] behind, which becomes the entry.

## My notes

title: What R means
text:
---
type: idea
---
# What R means

Results are measured in R, meaning "times the amount risked". If you risk £500 and win £1,000, that's +2R. If you lose the £500, that's −1R. Each trade risks 1% of the account, so +1R adds 1%. "After costs" takes off a small amount (0.05R) per trade for fees.

# Edge report

> [!info]
> Worked out automatically from 203 possible trades for the main strategy (taken and skipped) and 0 order-block trades. A group needs at least 8 trades to show up. Nothing here is proven yet; it shows where to look.

## The two strategies

- [[The main strategy]]: 23 trades, +7.00R, won 43%
- [[The order-block strategy]]: 0 trades, 0.00R, won 0%

## Doing best

| looking at | group | trades | won | per trade | total |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| sweep | breakout | 22 | 59% | +0.73R | +16.03R |
| time | 03:00 | 30 | 57% | +0.70R | +21.00R |
| direction | sells | 79 | 44% | +0.37R | +29.22R |
| session | London | 107 | 43% | +0.29R | +31.00R |
| time | 04:00 | 35 | 43% | +0.29R | +10.00R |

## Losing the most

|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| time | 08:00 | 9 | 0% | -1.00R | -9.00R |
| level | 15m high or low | 19 | 11% | -0.61R | -11.64R |
| session | NY | 96 | 17% | -0.48R | -45.87R |
| day | Thu | 63 | 14% | -0.47R | -29.34R |
| time | 09:00 | 83 | 17% | -0.46R | -38.39R |
| direction | buys | 124 | 22% | -0.36R | -44.09R |

## Is each check helping?

- An important level to target: skipped 48 trades that would have made +3.00R. So this check cost money.
- Price swept it and came back: skipped 9 trades that would have made +9.00R. So this check cost money.
- Matches the day's direction: skipped 23 trades that would have made +7.00R. So this check cost money.
- The other market disagreed (SMT): skipped 0 trades that would have made 0.00R. Too few to tell.
- The trend clearly flipped: skipped 0 trades that would have made 0.00R. Too few to tell.
- Price came back to the entry: skipped 0 trades that would have made 0.00R. Too few to tell.

## Things that don't add up

- The [[SMT]] check is earning its place: +0.09R a trade with it (65 trades) vs -0.34R without (69).
- The "important level" check holds up: important levels -0.04R a trade (149) vs minor ones -0.16R (54).
- The [[Grades]] work: A+ and A++ -0.12R a trade (30) vs B and C -0.14R (113).

## What's missing

- 23 trades is far too few. Anything under about 100 could flip either way.
- Everything uses 5-minute candles. 2-minute data starts 2026-09-08.
- Big news releases aren't filtered, fees are estimated, and entries assume a perfect fill.
- Rules: [[Rulebook v1.0]].

# Changelog

## v1.0: frozen, stress-tested (20 Oct 2026)

- **Rules frozen** for the forward test and the AI experiment. See the pre-registration.
- **Stress test** after a harsh outside review: limit orders now need price to trade a full tick through; stops slip (3 ticks in the first 15 minutes); real per-market costs on every trade; no trading on contract roll days; no new trades 8:25–8:40; flat before 2pm on Fed days.
- **Result: the main strategy's edge disappeared** (from +40.8R to −16.3R) and it failed the 2021–23 exam it had passed. The opening range on the Nasdaq held up (Sharpe 0.68 vs 0.02 for random entries), but the portfolio's Sharpe fell to 0.52 and buy-and-hold Nasdaq did better.
- **Deflated Sharpe:** after allowing for ~33,000 versions tried, the chance the portfolio's edge is real is about 0.3%. Most of the earlier edge was generous fills plus the luck of many tries.
- Added data checks (the 9:30 open must line up), confidence ranges, Sortino, buy-and-hold and random-entry benchmarks, and whole micro contracts.

## v0.10

- **The portfolio is now the main strategy plus the opening range on the Nasdaq**, 0.5% risk each. On 5 years of real futures: Sharpe 0.98 (better than either alone, because they barely move together), about +20% a year, worst drop about −40%.
- **The S&P opening range was dropped.** Sharpe 0.33; adding it lowered the portfolio's Sharpe from 0.98 to 0.84.
- **Volatility-scaled sizing was tested and rejected.** Risking less after wild months lowered the Sharpe (0.98 to 0.92) and made the worst drop deeper.
- Cleaned up the design: no gradient text, no glow, no animated borders, no fade-ins, no cursor glow, no badges above headings.

## v0.9

# Lessons

What Claude learned from testing on 1487 days of prices (2021-01-04 to 2026-10-01). Rewritten after every test. If you disagree with one, say why in your notes.

1. **A longer test changed the picture.** On the 63 months each version hadn't been tuned on, the old fixed rules lost +20.52R on [[The main strategy]] and -215.35R on [[The order-block strategy]].
2. **Adjusting every month helped, but didn't make it reliable.** Re-picking the best settings each month from the 6 months before cut the main strategy's loss to -16.31R and turned the order-block strategy to -21.28R. But the main strategy's rules changed in 27 of 63 months. When the "best" settings keep changing, that usually means chasing recent luck, not finding something that lasts.
3. **Hindsight is a trap.** The single best version over the whole period made +39.88R on the test months. You can only find it after the fact. Picked month by month, nothing came close.
4. **There's no magic lookback.** Looking back 3, 6, 9 or 12 months gave anything from -53.31R to -53.12R for the main strategy and -42.93R to -22.97R for the order-block one. No setting is reliably good, so we stay with 6 months, which was chosen before testing. Picking the best one now would just be overfitting again.
5. **Where the old rules lost most:** the Russell 2000 (-28.08R over 93 trades) and the London session (-1.93R).
6. **This month's rules (v1.0)** come from the last 6 months. Main strategy: +18.51R over 30 trades. Order-block strategy: +14.27R over 61 trades. Expect them to change again next month.
7. **A clock bug was hiding the result.** The free history is stamped in New York time with daylight saving, but it had been read as winter time, so for about 8 months of every year everything was an hour late: the New York window was really testing 7:30 to 10:30am. Fixed, the main strategy adjusting monthly went from losing to -16.31R over 407 trades on months it wasn't tuned on. That's encouraging, but it's roughly a 1 in 7 chance a strategy with no edge would look this good by luck, so it still needs the unseen 2021 to 2023 futures and the forward test before launch.
8. **Moving the stop to entry once a trade is +1R didn't help** in earlier tests, so it's switched off.
9. **Now trading the same markets as Kronos indices:** the Nasdaq, S&P 500, Dow and Russell 2000. Only the Nasdaq and S&P 500 have years of history for the long test; the Dow and Russell are only judged on the recent futures data until more is saved.
10. **More settings stopped helping; fixing the data did.** Before the clock fix, 24,600 versions couldn't make it profitable. The fix did. Data quality mattered more than any setting.
11. **The best idea came from published research, not from tweaking.** The opening-range breakout from Zarattini and Aziz's paper, with settings re-picked monthly and real trading costs taken off, made +144.80R on the Nasdaq over 63 months it hadn't seen. ICT's Silver Bullet hours made the sweep strategy worse, and the Judas swing looked good but only on 19 trades. On the last 50 days of real futures, the opening range lost money on the Dow and Russell, so it only runs on the Nasdaq and S&P until there's more history.
12. **Learning from mistakes cut the losses but didn't create an edge.** Tagging every losing setup and avoiding the mistakes that kept costing money took "take every setup" from -601.70R to -240.20R on months it hadn't seen. A first version of this looked like +98R, because it used losses that hadn't finished yet. Fixed, it's honest.
13. **Bottom line: no proven edge yet.** The forward test in November, on days nobody has seen, is what decides whether this goes live.

Changes are logged in the [[Changelog]]. Current rules: [[Rulebook v1.0]].

# Rulebook v0.10

The current rules, in plain English. Every month the settings are re-picked from whatever worked best over the previous 6 months (see [[Lessons]] for why that's not a guarantee). Every change is written in the [[Changelog]].

## [[The main strategy]]

1. **Pick a level.** It has to be an important one: a [[Session levels|session level]], a 15-minute or hourly high or low, or two near-equal highs or lows.
2. **Wait for a sweep.** Price must poke past it and close back within 10 minutes, during London 2–5am only.
3. **Day's direction:** only trade in the same direction as yesterday (sell if yesterday fell, buy if it rose).
4. **Markets disagree ([[SMT]]):** not required.
5. **Trend flip.** Within 40 minutes, with a big candle.
6. **Entry.** Wait for price to come back to the [[Price gap (FVG)|price gap]] (or the order block if there's no gap). Give up after an hour, or if price hits the target first.
7. **Risk rules** (from Argon v1, can't be switched off): the target must be worth at least 1.5× the risk, no more than 5 trades a day, stop for the day after losing 2R, one trade per market at a time.

Stop loss just past the sweep. Target: 2× the risk. Markets: Nasdaq, S&P 500 and gold. Everything closes at 3:55pm.

## [[The order-block strategy]]

Buy or sell the first time price comes back to a fresh 15-minute order block, if the hourly trend agrees. Markets: Nasdaq only. Session: New York 8:30–10am only. Same risk rules.

## Settings Claude is allowed to change

- **entry**: fvg_first, ob_first, ob_only
- **windows**: both, ny, london
- **bias**: none, h1, pd, h1_pd
- **smt**: required, optional
- **pool**: quality, any
- **markets**: all, nq, nq_es
- **target**: pool, 2R, 3R
